hall.does: build a hall: the greatest room, floor for many beds, a hearth, stores and fittings, and the most places for lines on its walls
hall.aware: the great room of a house, for many people
hall.rough: Timber on a stone footing, or stone, never wattle; stone is a mason's walling. All the materials go in first: short of one, nothing begins.
hall.capable: It needs free building ground, and a hall wants much of it: clear more first. The work runs over many days, more an act with skill; hungry, you do less.
hall.known: Added to a standing house it costs a quarter less. Finished, it is bare floor until fitted. Stone wears least in weather and holds a break-in off longest.

hand mill.does: build a hand mill: a quern in a house, where grain is ground by hand into meal for porridge, not bread
hand mill.aware: a quern for grinding grain by hand
hand mill.rough: Fitted inside a finished building, taking a little floor; name it, else it goes in your home here. With no free floor it is refused.
hand mill.capable: Grinding at it takes little grain an act, and its meal makes porridge only: bread wants flour from millstones or a water mill.
hand mill.known: It never wears, as millstones do, so it serves for small grindings even where a mill stands. A spoilt start loses its stone.

hearth.does: build a hearth: a fire in the house that warms it at night, cooks the household's raw food, bakes bread and dries meat or fish on its rack
hearth.aware: a fire in a house, for warmth and cooking
hearth.rough: A mason's work in stone, fitted inside a building, one to a building; never in a smokehouse or a camp.
hearth.capable: It warms only so much floor, so a large house is part cold. It burns the house's store, then the woodpile at the door; with neither, it stays cold.
hearth.known: A cold night burns several times a mild one's wood: keep a woodshed full. A smoke loft hangs above it, and an anvil needs one beside it.

medium room.does: build a medium room: floor for a household's beds, hearth and stores, and places for a few lines on its walls
medium room.aware: a middling room for a household's house
medium room.rough: Timber on a stone footing, or stone; too large for wattle. In timber it is a carpenter's work, in stone a mason's walling.
medium room.capable: Built onto a house here it costs a quarter less and needs ground beside it; a new house needs free building ground. More skill, more work done an act.
medium room.known: In a stone house it can go on an upper storey, taking no ground, never larger than the floor below. A wattle house must be rebuilt in timber first.

millstones.does: build dressed millstones: an ox mill, where an ox turns the stones and grain is ground to flour for bread, in large batches
millstones.aware: great stones turned by an ox to grind flour
millstones.rough: A mason's work and heavy: it goes on the ground floor of a finished building with floor to spare. Milling there needs an ox.
millstones.capable: Grinding wears the stones: past their life they grind half as much until dressed again. A water wheel can turn them in place of the ox.
millstones.known: Dress them as soon as they grind slow. Beside a river, add a water wheel: it grinds far more an act and needs no ox.

oven.does: build a stone oven: bread baked in great batches, a firing at a time, far more than a hearth bakes
oven.aware: a stone oven for baking bread in batches
oven.rough: A mason's work, fitted only in a stone building, taking some floor; in wattle or timber it is refused.
oven.capable: Each firing takes a full batch of flour, not meal, and firewood. After some firings it cracks and bakes half a batch until relined.
oven.known: A firing wants its whole batch of flour to hand, so it pays only where a mill keeps flour coming. Keep stone in hand to reline it.

owl hole.does: build an owl hole: a gap high in the gable where a barn owl may come to nest; nesting there, it keeps down the mice and rats in that building's store
owl hole.aware: a nesting gap for a barn owl, against mice
owl hole.rough: Cut into a finished building, taking no floor. No owl comes to a building where people sleep.
owl hole.capable: An owl takes the hole only at the turn of spring, and not every year. Once in, it stops more mice than rats in that one store.
owl hole.known: Best in a barn or granary nobody sleeps in, and it guards that building only. A dog or a cat does more against rats.

small room.does: build a small room: the least house, floor for a few beds, a hearth and bins, in wattle, timber or stone
small room.aware: the smallest room: a hut, or a house's first room
small room.rough: Wattle wants only timber and withies; stone is a mason's walling. It goes on built ground or scrub, never on field, pasture or wood.
small room.capable: The materials go in at the start, the work over days, more an act with skill. Finished, it is bare floor: beds, a hearth and bins make it a house.
small room.known: Wattle wears fastest in weather but mends for work alone; timber and stone wear slower and mend with their own stuff. Stone holds off a break-in longest.

smoke racks.does: build smoke racks: hurdles over a smouldering fire in a building of their own, where fish and meat are hung to smoke and keep
smoke racks.aware: racks for smoking fish and meat
smoke racks.rough: They go in a building with no beds or hearth, leaving floor free to work the fire; in a house they are refused.
smoke racks.capable: More sets hang more, as the floor allows. Tend the fire daily, fed from the store or the woodpile at the door, or the hanging waits, going off as fresh.
smoke racks.known: A hard cure wants a timber or stone smokehouse. Its fire can catch and spread to buildings on the same ground: keep it apart from houses, and not wattle.

stalls.does: build stalls: beasts housed through the winter, one a stall, eating less fodder, their dung kept on the ground, and not driven off past a barred door
stalls.aware: stalls to house beasts through the winter
stalls.rough: Built in a finished building on the ground where the herd stands, one held by the herd's people; each stall takes floor, ground floor only.
stalls.capable: Only the share of the herd with a stall is housed, so build one a head. They count in winter alone, and not in a ruined building.
stalls.known: Stalls on other ground than the herd do nothing: bring the herd to the byre's ground for winter. The dung kept there can be gathered for the fields.

standing stone.does: raise a standing stone: a monument with no room, on whose faces lines can be painted, carved or cut for those who come to it
standing stone.aware: a great stone set up as a monument
standing stone.rough: A mason's work, raised anywhere but in water; on building ground it takes a little of it. Its stone is all taken first.
standing stone.capable: Raised fine, rich or grand it costs far more stone and work, and is noticed further off. Cutting a line into it needs a mason and a tool.
standing stone.known: Its lines are read by those who work or speak at it. A line cut in stone costs more work to change or erase than paint.

vault.aware: a fireproof stone room for what must not burn
vault.rough: A mason's work: it needs a finished building and free building ground for its own room. All its stone is taken at the start.
vault.capable: It holds little for its cost, so keep there what a fire would ruin; the household's book can say what is kept in it.
vault.known: A fire takes the rest of the store but not the vault. It does not keep out rats and mice, nor the damp that spoils grain and cured goods.

water wheel.does: build a water wheel and leat: a water mill, where the river turns the millstones and grain is ground to flour in the largest batches
water wheel.aware: a mill wheel turned by the river
water wheel.rough: A carpenter's work, set in a building by water that already has dressed millstones; without the stones, or away from water, it is refused.
water wheel.capable: It wants copper and much timber and stone, and many days' work. The leat silts up within the year: then it grinds half until the leat is cleared.
water wheel.known: Where fish run, shut hatches grind at full but hold a run back below the dam; open, they grind half. Held fish are easier taken by hand.

weir.does: build a fish weir across a river with a crew: stakes and wattle that turn the fish runs into wicker traps in its gap, which fill by night
weir.aware: stakes across a river that trap fish as they run
weir.rough: Crew work across a river: name who builds it with you. One weir to a place; its first section is wattle unless you say timber.
weir.capable: Lift the catch often: full traps take no more. Shut, its gap takes the runs; open, very little. Floods and ice wear it, a shut gap in high water most.
weir.known: Add sections and stone footings to take more and wear less; timber outlasts wattle. Mend it a section at a time. Taking from another crew's weir is theft, and seen.

woodshed.aware: a lean-to for stacking fuel and timber
woodshed.rough: Put against a finished building, taking ground beside it, not floor; with no free building ground there it is refused.
woodshed.capable: It holds only timber, firewood and charcoal. It is part of the house's store, so the hearth burns from it first.
woodshed.known: Without one, a winter's fuel crowds the floor and spills outside the door, where it still burns but lies open to anyone.

angle.does: fish open water with a line: you take the water's own fish one by one into your hands
angle.aware: fishing with a hook and line
angle.rough: You need a hand line, or a rod and line, in your hands; with no line, or the bank iced, it is refused.
angle.capable: A rod takes more than a hand line. Every try wears the line: mend its hooks before it gives out. Fished hard, a water gives less until it recovers.
angle.known: The catch goes by luck about the mean, good days and poor. Fresh fish go off fast: eat, salt, dry or smoke them the same day.

cut.does: cut young growth in a wood or scrub for firewood: poles and brush, which grow back while beasts are kept off
cut.aware: cutting brush and poles for firewood
cut.rough: You need a tool in your hands; bare hands cannot. Ground with no young growth left is refused until it grows again.
cut.capable: A copper tool cuts more than a crude one, and every cut wears it. Beasts on the ground stop the regrowth while they are there.
cut.known: Growth comes back fastest on ground cut to about half, slowest when stripped bare. Where no willow grows, cutting withies draws on the same growth.

cut withies.does: cut withies: green rods from willow, or from young growth where no willow grows, for wattle, baskets, hurdles and wicker traps
cut withies.aware: cutting willow rods for wattle and wicker
cut withies.rough: Better with a tool than bare hands. A bed cut back is refused until it regrows; cut in leaf, it gives little.
cut withies.capable: A copper tool cuts more, and every cut wears it. Beasts on the ground halve the willow's regrowth. Rods from young growth come out of the wood's fuel.
cut withies.known: Willow cut in summer harms the stools: they bear less for years, mending slowly each spring. Withies keep a long while, so cut ahead of need.

den work.does: dig out a beast's den, or trap at a lodge, where you know one to be
den work.aware: digging out foxes, or trapping beavers at their lodge
den work.rough: Done where a beast keeps a den, earth, holt or lodge; where none is, you take nothing. A weapon helps a little.
den work.capable: At a beaver lodge you trap one an act, its pelt and castoreum; each taken shrinks the lodge. Elsewhere it is a hunt at the den, wearing your weapon.
den work.known: The last beaver taken ends the lodge for good, so leave some. Knowing the beasts of a place makes each take likelier.

dung.does: gather dung where beasts have stood, to spread on a field as manure
dung.aware: collecting beasts' dung for the fields
dung.rough: Done on pasture, meadow or field where beasts have been; where little lies it is refused.
dung.capable: Dung lies only where beasts stand, more where they are stalled in winter, and it does not wash away, so gather it when it suits.
dung.known: Manuring a field takes the dung from your hands or the store. Beasts grazing stubble or fallow feed the soil without your gathering.

fell.does: fell standing trees for timber, leaving their branches on the ground as dead wood
fell.aware: cutting down trees for building timber
fell.rough: Done in standing woodland, with a tool; bare hands do almost nothing. A wood with no standing timber left is refused.
fell.capable: A copper tool fells far more than a crude one, and felling wears a tool fast. Trees grow back slowly; a wood felled far down turns to scrub.
fell.known: Scrub takes buildings, and the brash feeds the firewood gatherers. Felling by a heronry while they nest may drive the herons off for good. Timber is heavy.

firewood.does: gather dead wood by hand from a wood or scrub, for the fire
firewood.aware: picking up dead wood for the fire
firewood.rough: Done by hand in a wood or scrub; picked clean of dead wood, it is refused until more falls.
firewood.capable: The thinner the dead wood lies, the less a search finds. Felling's brash and trees thrown by gales are fresh dead wood; old wood rots away.
firewood.known: Dead wood is anyone's: taking it from another's wood is not counted against you. Where it is thin, cut young growth instead.

fish by hand.does: fish the shallows at the water's edge by hand, spear or hand net, and take from a run of fish when one is passing
fish by hand.aware: catching small fish in the shallows by hand
fish by hand.rough: Done at the edge of water or fen; with the edges iced, or the shallows fished out and nothing running, it is refused.
fish by hand.capable: A dip net in your hands takes far more from a run where the water narrows. The shallows refill over time; fished bare, they give little.
fish by hand.known: Below a mill's shut dam a run going up is held, and easier to take. Knowing the fish of these waters makes each take likelier.

forage.rough: Done by hand on rough or wild ground; where the place is picked bare, it is refused.
forage.capable: The more stands, the more a day finds; picked hard, a place gives little until it grows back, slower in winter.
forage.known: Spread the picking over many places so each keeps coming back. Wild food keeps only a few days: eat it, or give it while fresh.

gather wild food.does: gathering the wild food there is where you are
gather wild food.aware: gathering whatever wild food is in season
gather wild food.rough: Done by hand on wild or rough ground; with nothing in season there, it is refused. Mushrooms you do not know can make you ill.
gather wild food.capable: Say what you are looking for, nuts, berries or mushrooms, and you take more of it and less of the rest. The more stands, the more you find.
gather wild food.known: Practice makes bad mushrooms rarer, and an expert never takes one; the unpractised may die of them. Wild beasts eat the same plants on your land.

gather young.does: take the young from the nests of a colony
gather young.aware: taking young herons or rooks from their nests
gather young.rough: Only where a heronry or rookery stands, and only while there are young in the nests; otherwise you take nothing.
gather young.capable: Each visit takes a share of the nests, more with skill, and the colony is smaller after. Herons troubled at their nests may leave for good.
gather young.known: Rooks stay however you work them, and fewer rooks do less harm to the young corn beside them. Herons do not: take lightly, and never fell there.

hay.does: cut grass on a meadow or pasture for hay: fodder kept to feed beasts when the grass is gone
hay.rough: Best with a tool; bare hands cut little. Grass grazed too short is refused, and a cut in winter gives nothing.
hay.capable: A copper tool cuts more, and every cut wears it. Hay taken leaves less grass for the herd there, though grass grows back fast in good months.
hay.known: Hay keeps well in store, and a hungry herd draws on its holders' stores. Stalled beasts make the winter's hay go further.

hunt.does: hunt game in a wood: a chance of a kill, its meat and sometimes its hide
hunt.aware: hunting deer and game in the woods
hunt.rough: Done in woodland, and many hunts come home empty. Carry a weapon: unarmed, even a kill brings home little.
hunt.capable: The thicker the game, the likelier a kill. A weapon and practice bring home more from each kill; the weapon wears. Hunted too hard, game may not return.
hunt.known: Sometimes the hide comes home with the meat. Fresh meat goes off within days: cook, salt, dry or smoke it, or share it.

hunt the wild.does: go out after whatever game the place holds, and take what you meet
hunt the wild.aware: going out into the wild after whatever game there is
hunt the wild.rough: Done on wild ground away from water. Carry a weapon: without one, most beasts you meet get away.
hunt the wild.capable: Practice raises the odds far more than in other crafts. Game hunted often grows wary and flees sooner. Boar, wolves and bears can turn and hurt you.
hunt the wild.known: What you cannot carry is cut and left, drawing scavengers: lead a pack ox, or hunt with others. Say what you are looking for, and how far to range.

hunting drive.does: beat a wood with others to drive beasts onto waiting spears: it needs others with you (a party you lead, or another's you join with "with")
hunting drive.aware: a drive of beaters and spears after boar and deer
hunting drive.rough: It needs others with you, in a party you lead or join; alone it is refused. Spears in hand help greatly.
hunting drive.capable: Each one out past the first raises the odds. A beast that turns hurts one of those out, so more hands spread the danger. Practice counts for much.
hunting drive.known: A drive takes large beasts, more meat than a party can carry: the rest is cut and left. Herons nesting by a driven wood may leave.

mine.does: dig copper ore from a seam in the rock, for a smith to smelt into copper
mine.aware: digging copper ore out of the rock
mine.rough: A miner's work at a seam in rock, with a tool in your hands; without one it is refused.
mine.capable: A copper tool digs more, and mining wears a tool very fast. A seam does not grow back: once worked out, it is gone for good.
mine.known: Ore weighs far more than the copper it gives: smelting takes several ore and much fuel. Dig what the smith can smelt and carry.

net.does: spread nets and decoys where birds come down, and take what you net
net.aware: catching wildfowl with nets and decoys
net.rough: Done on fen, water, meadow or saltmarsh where birds come down; it takes only what flies.
net.capable: Nets by the water take more than on dry ground, and no weapon helps. Birds netted often grow wary and lift sooner.
net.known: Knowing the fowl of a place makes each take likelier; practice counts for less than in the hunt.

quarry.does: quarry stone from a rock face, for walls, hearths, ovens and stone houses
quarry.aware: cutting building stone from the rock
quarry.rough: A mason's work at a rock face, with a tool in your hands; without one it is refused.
quarry.capable: A copper tool cuts more, and quarrying wears a tool very fast. A face never runs out, however much is taken.
quarry.known: Stone is heavy and a stone house wants a great deal of it: quarry close to where you build.
